question: What does a psychoactive substance mainly do to the human body?

options.A: It permanently repairs damaged nerve tissues
options.B: It alters brain function and mental state
options.C: It lowers overall blood pressure immediately
options.D: It speeds up the process of digestion

explanation: Spot on! Psychoactive substances target the central nervous system, which changes how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. You've got this! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h1)

question: How do we best describe substance intoxication in clinical practice?

options.A: A mild nutritional deficiency resulting from poor diet
options.B: A permanent physical injury caused by chemical toxicity
options.C: A temporary, reversible impairment of mental and physical function
options.D: A lifelong genetic disorder of the central nervous system

explanation: You nailed it! Intoxication is a short-term, reversible state that happens right after someone takes a psychoactive substance. It passes as the body clears the drug. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h1)

question: Which brain chemical is most closely linked to the reward system and feelings of pleasure?
explanation: Great job! Dopamine is the brain's main messenger for making us feel good and reinforcing rewarding behaviors. Think of it as the brain's natural 'feel-good' chemical. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h2)

question: Why does the brain cut back on its own chemical receptors after repeated drug use?

options.A: To increase the speed of normal digestion
options.B: To store extra energy for physical exercise
options.C: To improve overall visual acuity at night
options.D: To protect itself from chemical overload

explanation: Well thought out! When a drug floods the brain, it tries to protect itself by reducing receptors (down-regulation) to restore some balance. The body is always trying to keep things stable! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h2)

question: Which of these common substances acts as a Central Nervous System (CNS) depressant?
explanation: Correct! Alcohol slows down brain activity, making it a depressant. Remember: depressants slow things down, while stimulants speed them up. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h3)

question: A patient in the emergency ward has a racing heart, high blood pressure, and extreme restlessness after taking a drug. What kind of drug is most likely behind this?
explanation: Spot on! Stimulants like cocaine or amphetamines rev up the nervous system, leading to high energy, fast heart rates, and agitation. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h3)

question: In drug use, what does the term 'tolerance' actually mean?

options.A: Experiencing severe pain when the substance is stopped
options.B: Being able to break down alcohol faster than normal
options.C: Feeling angry when people talk about substance use
options.D: Needing a higher dose to get the same physical or mental effect

explanation: You got it! Tolerance happens when the body gets so used to a substance that the usual amount doesn't work anymore, so the person needs more to feel the same effect. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h4)

question: Why do people stopping heavy alcohol use often experience dangerous symptoms like shaking (tremors) and seizures?

options.A: The brain experiences a rebound effect of hyperexcitability
options.B: The liver fails to filter out toxins quickly enough
options.C: The stomach lining becomes irritated by lack of nutrients
options.D: The muscles lose all stored protein and water

explanation: Brilliant! Since alcohol depresses the brain, taking it away suddenly causes the nervous system to bounce back hard and become dangerously overactive. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is the main reason nurses use screening tools like the CAGE questionnaire?

options.A: To measure the exact blood alcohol concentration
options.B: To diagnose clinical depression and anxiety
options.C: To test liver function enzymes in the blood
options.D: To quickly screen for potential alcohol use problems

explanation: Spot on! CAGE is a quick, easy set of questions that helps us spot clients who might be struggling with alcohol, so we can support them early. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h5)

question: During a hospital admission assessment, what is a vital detail to find out about a patient's substance history?

options.A: The date and time of their last dose
options.B: How much money they spend each month
options.C: The name of the friend who introduced them
options.D: Their personal opinion on local drug laws

explanation: You're doing great! Knowing when they last used helps you predict and prepare for any withdrawal symptoms that might pop up during their stay. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h5)

question: What is the very first nursing priority when caring for a patient who is heavily intoxicated?

options.A: Asking the patient to sign a treatment contract
options.C: Exploring childhood causes of substance use
options.D: Teaching about the long-term dangers of drugs

explanation: Correct! Always remember your ABCs first. Keeping the patient breathing and stable is always our top emergency priority before anything else. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h6)

question: Why do nurses use rating scales like the CIWA-Ar for patients going through alcohol withdrawal?

options.A: To objectively measure symptom severity and guide medication doses
options.B: To determine the exact legal penalties for public intoxication
options.C: To replace the need for physical and neurological exams
options.D: To punish the patient for failing to stop drinking

explanation: Spot on! These scales take the guesswork out of care, helping us give the right medications safely and only when the patient truly needs them. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h6)

question: Which of these phrases is an example of respectful, person-first language in mental health nursing?

options.A: A chronic alcoholic clogging the ward
options.B: A substance abuser who lacks willpower
options.C: A person with a substance use disorder

explanation: You nailed it! Person-first language puts the human being before the medical condition, reminding us to treat every patient with dignity and respect. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of harm reduction strategies in community nursing?

options.A: To minimize negative health and social consequences of drug use
options.B: To force every patient into immediate inpatient rehab
options.C: To arrest individuals who possess illegal substances
options.D: To ignore drug use until the person asks for help

explanation: Great thinking! Harm reduction is all about keeping people safe, preventing infections, and saving lives—meeting patients right where they are with compassion. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T5#GNS223_U6_T5_h7)
